title: Development of the Neural Tube

items.text: The axial mesodermal notochord provides inductive signals to overlying ectoderm, initiating neural plate development.
Plate bending creates a groove bounded by folds; fusion produces the tube and separates it from the future epidermis.
SHH from notochord and floor plate patterns ventral neural tissue; the deck also names BMP/TGF-beta and Wnt pathways as participants in neurulation.

Roof-plate/overlying ectoderm BMP signaling favors dorsal identities, whereas notochord/floor-plate SHH favors ventral identities. Wnt pathways also participate in plate shaping and regional patterning.
Ventral basal plate develops motor regions, while dorsal alar plate contributes sensory processing regions; this is a high-yield extension of SHH/BMP patterning.

qualifications: SHH is the classic ventral patterning signal; dorsal BMP/TGF-beta and Wnt pathways also participate. Neural induction is not identical to subsequent dorsal–ventral patterning.

items.text: Closure begins near the future cervical region and progresses toward the cranial and caudal ends.
These are the deck's approximate embryonic ages; closure is normally completed by the end of week 4.
The neural canal persists as the CSF-containing ventricular system and central canal; the tube wall becomes CNS tissue.
The telencephalon is a secondary forebrain vesicle and produces the hemispheres surrounding the lateral ventricles.
The diencephalon surrounds the third ventricle and gives rise to these forebrain structures, including the neural retina.
The mesencephalon remains the midbrain, and its narrow cavity becomes the cerebral aqueduct.
The rostral secondary hindbrain vesicle forms pons and cerebellum and contributes to the fourth ventricular cavity.
Myelencephalon is the caudal secondary hindbrain vesicle; its cavity contributes to the fourth ventricle and transition to the central canal.

title: Neural Crest

items.text: EMT permits crest cells to delaminate and migrate into peripheral and craniofacial sites. Timing varies by region; cranial migration can begin before complete tube closure.
Sensory ganglia, peripheral glia, and chromaffin cells are classic neural crest derivatives shown in the source diagram.
Crest cells normally form enteric ganglia; failure to populate distal bowel causes Hirschsprung disease, a related application of the diagram's enteric nervous system derivative.
Pigment cells and dentin-producing odontoblasts are crest derivatives; enamel-producing ameloblasts instead arise from oral ectoderm.
These structures develop from neural tube neuroectoderm, with retina and posterior pituitary associated with forebrain outgrowths.
Lens/corneal epithelium and epidermal appendages derive from surface ectoderm; oral and otic ectoderm produce adenohypophysis/enamel and inner ear, respectively.

The source chart lists these endodermal epithelia, together with middle-ear/auditory-tube/tonsillar epithelia and much of bladder/urachal lining. Surrounding connective tissues can have other origins.
Intermediate mesoderm supplies urogenital organs, ducts, and associated structures.
These are the diagram's broad derivative groups. Blood/lymph lineages, spleen, and adrenal cortex are mesodermal; cranial connective tissue also has substantial neural crest contributions.
Cranial ectomesenchyme is crest-derived, so the diagram's broad 'head mesoderm/dentin' grouping should not override the specific odontoblast lineage.

qualifications: The original diagram is retained unchanged. Its dentin/head-mesoderm grouping is simplified: odontoblasts are cranial neural crest-derived. Cranial crest migration can start before full tube closure, so the timing bullet is not universal. Cranial sensory ganglia may have both placodal and crest contributions.

items.text: Anencephaly follows failure of cranial neural tube closure and involves severe loss of cerebral hemispheres and calvarium.
Failure of posterior closure is associated with open spinal dysraphism. A simple closed vertebral arch defect is distinguished from exposed neural tissue.

title: Spina Bifida

items.text: A bony posterior arch defect without meningeal/neural herniation is the defining finding; some cutaneous markers warrant evaluation for occult dysraphism.
The sac contains meninges and CSF without spinal cord; neurologic deficits are often absent but depend on associated abnormalities.
Myelomeningocele contains neural tissue and may cause motor, sensory, and bowel/bladder deficits; exposed tissue increases infection risk.
Myelomeningocele is strongly associated with Chiari II and hydrocephalus; this is a related NBME association beyond sac-content classification.

qualifications: Occulta is a closed vertebral arch defect; open neural lesions differ in sac contents and neurologic risk. Cutaneous markers can accompany more complex occult dysraphism.

items.text: A meningocele contains meninges/CSF, whereas a myelomeningocele contains neural tissue; location or external appearance alone cannot reliably establish contents.

title: Neural Tube Defects (NTDs): Risk Factors & Prevention

items.text: Closure occurs during the first month after fertilization, often before pregnancy recognition, so adequate folate must be present early.
The deck specifically identifies valproate and carbamazepine as associated with increased NTD risk; medication planning requires individualized clinical review.
NTDs are multifactorial: folate, medications such as carbamazepine/valproate, and genetic susceptibility all matter.
Open neural tissue can produce elevated amniotic AFP and acetylcholinesterase; AFP is a screening clue rather than a standalone diagnosis.
CDC recommends 400 micrograms daily; previous NTD pregnancy requires clinician-directed higher-dose planning rather than automatically using the average-risk amount.
Holoprosencephaly is defective forebrain cleavage, with severe forms producing cyclopia and other midline facial defects.
SHH is important in midline patterning, and trisomy 13 is a classic chromosomal association of holoprosencephaly.
Holoprosencephaly instead reflects failure of forebrain division; both can be severe, but the developmental mechanisms differ.
Lissencephaly is a cortical migration disorder; LIS1/PAFAH1B1 and DCX are classic associated genes.
Both participate in neuronal migration; variants can produce abnormal cortical gyration and neurodevelopmental impairment.
Microcephaly is an abnormally small head associated with impaired brain growth; genetic disorders and congenital infections are relevant causes.
Crest contributes extensively to arch cartilage, bone, connective tissue, and vascular smooth muscle; arch skeletal muscle is principally mesodermal.
The pharyngeal apparatus becomes apparent early in week 4 and develops through this interval.
The mandibular arch contributes these structures. Much of the mandible ossifies in crest-derived mesenchyme adjacent to Meckel cartilage rather than simply replacing that cartilage.
V3 provides branchial motor supply to first-arch muscles, including these muscles and the tensor muscles.
Both are first-arch muscles; tensor veli palatini is the important exception to most palate muscles being supplied by vagus.
Reichert cartilage of the second arch contributes this group; stapes fixation can impair sound transmission.
These are all supplied by CN VII, the second-arch nerve.
CN VII innervates facial expression, orbicularis oculi, and stapedius; these are second-arch muscles.
Reichert cartilage derivatives include stapes, styloid process, stylohyoid ligament, and upper/lesser-horn hyoid components.
The third arch forms this skeletal/muscle group; glossopharyngeal nerve also supplies gag afference.
Glossopharyngeal provides the classic gag afferent limb; its arch muscle is stylopharyngeus. This sensory role is distinct from vagal gag motor output.
Second contributes lesser horn/upper body, while third contributes greater horn/lower body.

title: Arches 4 & 6 (Laryngeal Arches)

items.text: Cricothyroid is a fourth-arch muscle innervated by this vagal branch; most other intrinsic laryngeal muscles use recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Sixth-arch muscles receive recurrent laryngeal innervation; cricothyroid is the fourth-arch exception.
These exceptions are common exam discriminators when interpreting broad vagal pharyngeal/palatal associations.
These arches contribute laryngeal skeletal elements; cartilage contributions can be complex, so the grouped framework is the useful relationship.

qualifications: Separate fourth-arch superior laryngeal/cricothyroid relationships from sixth-arch recurrent laryngeal/other intrinsic laryngeal muscles. Stylopharyngeus and tensor veli palatini are important IX and V3 exceptions.

title: Skeletal Structures of the Head and Face

items.text: The diagram contrasts broad anterior crest and posterior mesodermal territories. Its label 'occipital somites' for all red areas is simplified; parietal bone is broadly paraxial mesodermal rather than entirely occipital-somite derived.
These facial bones are in the illustrated crest-derived region, along with much of the anterior skull and hyoid-related skeleton.

qualifications: The source color map is a broad crest-versus-mesoderm teaching schematic. Not all mesodermal skull territory is derived specifically from occipital somites.

items.text: Agnathia denotes absent mandible/extreme first-arch hypoplasia and can be incompatible with life; deficient crest contribution is the mechanism emphasized by the deck.
This constellation is mandibulofacial dysostosis, commonly involving TCOF1 and abnormal cranial crest development/survival.
TCOF1 is the most common association, and severity can vary; other genes/inheritance patterns exist, so this is the typical rather than exclusive pattern.
Malformed external/middle-ear structures impair sound transmission; a first-arch malformation need not damage cochlear hair cells to cause hearing loss.
Pierre Robin sequence begins with mandibular hypoplasia; secondary tongue-position effects disrupt palatal development and can impair feeding/breathing.
The tongue falls posteriorly in the setting of micrognathia, contributing to airway obstruction and interference with palate formation.
Each arch contains skeletal, muscle, arterial, and nerve components in this layered organization.
This distinction predicts derivatives such as middle ear from first pouch and external meatus from first cleft.
The left distal sixth arch forms ductus arteriosus; proximal sixth arches contribute pulmonary arteries. This extends the deck's artery-per-arch concept.
The third arch is carotid-associated; fourth forms left aortic arch/right proximal subclavian, while sixth is pulmonary/ductus-associated.

title: Pouches

items.text: The first pouch tubotympanic recess forms these endodermal epithelial spaces; the external canal instead comes from first cleft.
Second pouch contributes tonsillar epithelium and crypts; lymphocytes subsequently populate the tissue from hematopoietic lineages.
Inferior parathyroids descend with thymic tissue from third pouch, traveling farther than fourth-pouch superior glands and allowing ectopic locations.

The deck groups this with fourth pouch (sometimes termed fourth/fifth complex). Modern mammalian lineage evidence supports an endodermal C-cell origin; older charts often label them neural crest-derived.
The DiGeorge phenotype links thymic/parathyroid hypoplasia to T-cell deficiency and hypocalcemia, often in 22q11.2 deletion with conotruncal abnormalities.
Thymic epithelial development is necessary for normal T-cell maturation; third-pouch dysfunction can therefore impair cellular immunity.
The eardrum illustrates first membrane formation at the interface of external canal and middle-ear cavity.

qualifications: Pouch contributions refer principally to epithelial primordia, not every cell in the mature organ. C-cell contribution is through ultimobranchial bodies; modern mammalian lineage studies support endoderm rather than the older universal neural-crest assignment.

items.text: The first ectodermal cleft forms the external acoustic meatus; clefts 2–4 are normally overgrown and obliterated.
Persistence of second-cleft/cervical sinus tissue produces a lateral neck cyst, sinus, or fistula.
The location and behavior are characteristic of a branchial cleft cyst.
A fistula has two openings; a sinus has one opening, and a cyst is a closed cavity.
A single opening with a blind end is a sinus.
The thyroid primordium appears near this midline site in week 4 and descends into the neck through the thyroglossal tract.
Regression leaves the thyroid separated from the original tongue-base site; persistent tissue can form a cyst or ectopic gland.
The figure's pyramidal lobe is a thyroid-descent remnant; a cyst and lingual thyroid are other abnormalities related to this pathway.
Attachment along the thyroid's migration path accounts for characteristic midline position and movement.
Thyroid tissue can remain at the original tongue-base region; ectopic tissue may be the patient's only functioning thyroid.

title: Thyroglossal Duct Cyst vs. Branchial Cleft Cyst

items.text: These classic patterns distinguish thyroid-tract remnants from second-cleft/cervical sinus remnants, although real masses still require evaluation.
This is the five-prominence organization; maxillary and mandibular prominences are first-arch components.
The paired first-arch mandibular prominences contribute the lower face and jaw.
Maxillary prominences form these upper facial regions and also give rise to secondary palatal shelves.
Their merger produces the intermaxillary segment, including central upper lip/philtrum and primary palate.
Failure of this union produces the classic cleft lip.
The lateral nasal prominences contribute the nasal alae; medial prominences contribute the intermaxillary segment.
This is the primary palate; the incisive foramen is a key boundary with secondary palate.
The shelves elevate and fuse, forming the remaining hard palate and the soft palate.
These fusions establish the roof of the mouth and separation of oral/nasal spaces.
The shelves initially lie vertically; clearance by the descending tongue permits horizontal elevation and subsequent fusion.
Reduced mandibular space and glossoptosis interfere mechanically with normal shelf repositioning, as in Pierre Robin sequence.

title: Normal and Abnormal Development of the Lip and Palate

items.text: An isolated cleft palate can occur with a normal lip and causes feeding, regurgitation, and speech problems.
Primary palate is anterior to this landmark; secondary palate is posterior. Clefts can extend across this boundary.
This related image-based application distinguishes an oblique facial cleft from the more common maxillary–medial nasal cleft lip.
Their merger forms the central intermaxillary segment; failure can produce a median upper-lip cleft.
Lip defects concern facial prominence union; palatal defects concern shelves and their connections. Either may occur alone or together.

title: Layers of the Eyeball

items.text: Sclera provides protection and extraocular muscle attachment; transparent cornea is the major refractive surface.
These form the middle vascular layer, supporting nutrition, accommodation/aqueous production, and pupil control.
The choroid/choriocapillaris supplies the outer retina; the central retinal artery primarily supplies the inner retina.
Ciliary processes produce aqueous, and ciliary muscle changes zonular tension to alter lens shape.
This related anatomy explains why impaired anterior chamber angle drainage can increase intraocular pressure; aqueous originates in ciliary processes.
The small aqueous posterior chamber is not the large postremal/vitreous compartment; anterior chamber lies between cornea and iris.
The serrated retinal margin marks transition toward nonphotosensitive ciliary epithelium; vitreous occupies the large compartment behind the lens.
Rhegmatogenous detachment separates neurosensory retina from RPE, threatening photoreceptor support; this applies the illustrated retinal/choroidal layering.
Impaired aqueous outflow rapidly raises pressure, linking chamber/iris anatomy to a high-yield ocular emergency.

qualifications: Posterior aqueous chamber is distinct from the large vitreous/postremal chamber. Conventional aqueous outflow uses the trabecular meshwork and scleral venous sinus.

items.text: The air-cornea interface supplies most fixed refractive power; the lens provides adjustable focusing.
The ocular optical system reverses image orientation, so superior field projects inferiorly and right field onto left retinal halves.
A negative lens reduces effective convergence, moving the focus posteriorly onto the retina.
A less deformable lens cannot round adequately for near focus despite ciliary activation; this extends the slide's adjustable-focus concept.
Parasympathetic ciliary contraction reduces suspensory tension, increasing lens curvature and refractive power.
Preganglionic oculomotor fibers synapse in ciliary ganglion; postganglionic short ciliary fibers activate ciliary muscle.
Relaxation increases zonular traction and reduces lens curvature/power.
Circular sphincter contraction produces miosis; its efferent route differs from sympathetic dilation.
These fibers travel along the carotid/orbital pathway and chiefly through long ciliary nerves to produce mydriasis.
Loss of sympathetic dilation causes miosis in Horner syndrome; the deck's sympathetic iris pathway explains the pupil finding.
Muscarinic blockade prevents parasympathetic miosis and accommodation, causing mydriasis and cycloplegia.
Sympathetic postganglionic and sensory fibers pass through without using this ganglion as their autonomic synapse.
Retinal ganglion-cell axons converge at the optic disc to form CN II.
The fovea specializes in detailed central vision, whereas peripheral retina is more rod-rich.
The disc is an exit/entry site, so incident light at that retinal location cannot be directly detected.
Rods are highly sensitive for scotopic vision; cones support color and high spatial acuity, especially in fovea.
Phototransduction activates transducin/phosphodiesterase, lowering cGMP and decreasing glutamate release; darkness keeps cGMP-gated channels open.
The source fundus images show the disc/vessels nasally and the macula temporally; the macular center is fovea.
Damage to central high-acuity retina impairs reading and detailed fixation while peripheral retina can remain functional.

title: Normal disc versus papilledema

items.text: Papilledema is a pressure-related diagnosis, typically bilateral; other causes of disc edema must be distinguished.
The optic nerve is a CNS extension with meningeal coverings; raised pressure can impair axoplasmic transport at the disc.
Disc swelling can enlarge the blind spot; central acuity may be relatively preserved early, so a normal reading test does not exclude it.

qualifications: Papilledema means optic disc edema specifically due to raised intracranial pressure; the term does not cover every cause of a swollen disc.

items.text: Left space maps to the right half of each retina: nasal half in the left eye and temporal half in the right eye.
Vertical inversion places superior visual space on inferior retinal tissue, whose temporal radiation pathway includes Meyer's loop.
Right field maps to left retinal halves, and inferior field maps superiorly. Nasal right-eye fibers cross to join left temporal-eye fibers in the left pathway.
Horizontal image reversal maps temporal visual space onto nasal retina.
Nasal and temporal retinal halves in each eye receive opposite visual-space halves; the central region is binocular.
This is the deck's principal retinogeniculocalcarine pathway; not all retinal fibers terminate in LGN.
Most optic tract fibers relay in LGN before reaching cortex through optic radiations.
The light reflex does not require intact conscious visual cortex, unlike cortical perception of the image.
Crossing nasal fibers join uncrossed temporal retinal fibers from the opposite eye to encode a shared contralateral hemifield.
It contains crossed left nasal retinal fibers and uncrossed right temporal retinal fibers.
Both encode right visual space, with the nasal right-eye population crossing at chiasm.
Inferior retinal fibers loop through temporal lobe to inferior calcarine cortex; injury causes superior quadrantanopia.
The superior optic radiations travel parietally; their lesions cause inferior quadrantanopia.
Each LGN receives combined input from both eyes after chiasmal sorting and sends optic radiations to cortex on its own side.
V1/area 17 lies on the medial occipital surface around calcarine sulcus.
Superior bank/cuneus represents contralateral inferior visual field.
Inferior calcarine bank/lingual gyrus represents contralateral superior field.
Central vision is represented posteriorly with extensive cortical allocation; more anterior calcarine regions represent peripheral vision.

title: Visual Pathway: Three Rules for Localization

items.text: Inferior retina represents upper space, and left postchiasmal pathways carry right space; temporal fibers are Meyer's loop.
This avoids mistaking temporal visual field for temporal retina and keeps eye side distinct from hemifield side.
Prechiasmal lesions affect one eye; exact pattern depends on lesion extent and site.
This is a postchiasmal pattern; the affected hemifield is opposite the cerebral lesion.
The right optic nerve contains all afferent visual information from the right eye before chiasmal sorting.
Each nasal hemiretina detects its temporal field, so midline chiasmal compression by a pituitary mass causes bitemporal hemianopia.
Retinal location and visual-field location are opposite; this is the key step in the chiasm question.
The left tract carries right visual-space information from both eyes.
These encode the left hemifield and join within the right tract after nasal crossing.

title: Optic Radiations: Temporal vs Parietal Lesions

items.text: Left temporal inferior retinal fibers carry right superior visual-space information, producing 'pie in the sky' loss.
Right parietal superior retinal fibers encode left inferior space: 'pie on the floor.'
These patterns follow retinal inversion and ipsilateral radiation projections from LGN to V1.

title: Primary Visual Cortex Lesions

items.text: PCA supplies much medial occipital visual cortex; sparing of macular cortex can preserve central vision, and the light reflex can remain intact because it uses pretectal pathways.
This often supports occipital involvement with spared macular cortex, sometimes due to collateral supply, but is not obligatory or absolutely site-specific.
Posterior occipital cortex represents the macular field; more anterior regions represent peripheral visual space.

qualifications: Macular sparing is common in some occipital lesions, but is neither required nor perfectly specific. Sparing reflects preserved central-field representation, sometimes with collateral supply.

items.text: Parietal radiations carry contralateral inferior field information.
This affects input from only the right eye. Left tract, LGN, radiations, or V1 can produce right homonymous loss.
Testing each eye demonstrates a binocular hemifield deficit, supporting left postchiasmal localization.
Retinal ganglion axons carry the light signal through optic nerve pathways toward pretectal nuclei.
Bilateral central connections distribute one eye's light signal to both parasympathetic outputs, producing direct and consensual responses.
Its axons run with III and synapse in ciliary ganglion before reaching sphincter pupillae.
This orbital parasympathetic ganglion relays output to sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle.
The contralateral pupil constricts through bilateral pretectal–Edinger–Westphal connections.

title: Pupillary Light Reflex: CN II vs CN III Lesions

items.text: Left afferent input is absent, but both efferent pathways work when the right retina is stimulated.
An efferent defect prevents the affected pupil from responding to either eye's afferent stimulus; isolated parasympathetic injury may spare other III functions.
Normal left afference activates bilateral outputs, including a consensual response in the blind right eye.
Right retinal afference still reaches bilateral central nuclei, but only the intact left output can constrict its pupil.
Loss of III motor supply produces ptosis/down-and-out position, while efferent parasympathetic failure prevents left miosis with either afferent stimulus.
A compressive aneurysm can affect superficial III parasympathetic fibers; pupil findings are useful but do not by themselves exclude serious causes in pupil-sparing presentations.

qualifications: The source table models complete isolated afferent lesions and complete parasympathetic efferent failure. Partial lesions and pupil-sparing III palsies do not necessarily follow the complete-lesion table.

title: Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (Marcus Gunn Pupil)

items.text: The left eye supplies less afferent light input; both intact efferent outputs relax relative to the response driven by the healthier eye.
Optic neuritis is a classic cause of reduced afferent input; normal resting pupil size and intact III function are compatible with RAPD.
The deck's complete CN II table is an idealized extreme; partial optic nerve disease can still drive weaker bilateral constriction.

qualifications: RAPD describes asymmetric afferent drive, often with equal resting pupil sizes and intact efferent pathways. Severe asymmetric retinal disease can also cause it.

items.text: The lens rounds, medial recti turn both eyes inward, and sphincter pupillae constricts the pupils.
Bilateral III somatic motor output adducts both eyes toward a near target.
Miosis complements increased lens power and convergence; it is not the mechanism that changes lens curvature.

title: Neural Pathways of the Near Response

items.text: Both ultimately use III parasympathetic output for miosis, but their upstream circuitry differs.
Parasympathetic visceral motor output produces accommodation/miosis; somatic motor output produces convergence.
Its medial rectus neurons drive convergence; Edinger–Westphal supplies preganglionic parasympathetic pupil/lens output.

title: Light-Near Dissociation

items.text: The near response is preserved or relatively better despite impaired light-mediated constriction.
Small irregular pupils with light-near dissociation are the classic association emphasized by the slides.
Ciliary ganglion/short ciliary injury and aberrant reinnervation can produce tonic near responses; early near function may also be impaired.
Parinaud syndrome involves dorsal midbrain structures, including pupillary light pathways, and is classically associated with pineal-region compression.
Damage can preferentially affect light-reflex relays while relatively sparing supranuclear near pathways.

qualifications: Adie near constriction may be impaired early and becomes tonic with reinnervation. Light-near dissociation denotes a relative advantage of near over light constriction.

items.text: Corneal somatic sensory input activates bilateral facial motor output.
Bilateral facial motor nuclei activate eyelid closure; the branchial motor category is SVE.
One afferent corneal signal drives direct and consensual blink responses through bilateral motor connections.
Left sensory input is absent, but both VII outputs are demonstrably intact when right corneal input is provided.
The right efferent limb is defective, while sensory input from both corneas reaches the intact left motor output.
The sensory signal reaches both motor nuclei, but left facial output cannot activate orbicularis.
Peripheral VII dysfunction impairs ipsilateral blink output; preserved sensation distinguishes it from isolated V1 loss.
Angular head rotation changes vestibular afferent activity, initiating compensatory eye movements.
Eyes move opposite the head: left eye abducts via VI, and right eye adducts via III through internuclear connections.
The VI motor component drives ipsilateral lateral rectus while crossed internuclear input drives the other eye's medial rectus.
Compensatory eye movement limits retinal image slip and can operate without conscious visual processing, including in darkness.
The nucleus contains left lateral rectus motor neurons and internuclear neurons for right medial rectus via the MLF; a nerve lesion alone mainly impairs left abduction.

title: Oculocephalic Reflex (Doll's Eye Maneuver)

items.text: Compensatory movement opposite head rotation is the expected doll's-eye response in this context.
This can reflect dysfunction along vestibular/brainstem/ocular motor pathways; drugs and other confounders matter, so the maneuver alone does not establish brain death.
The source specifically cautions against oculocephalic testing when cervical instability is suspected.

qualifications: Absent doll’s-eye responses require context, including medication and peripheral pathway confounders; this single maneuver does not establish brain death. Avoid head rotation with suspected cervical instability.

items.text: The paired tract links vestibular and ocular motor nuclei and coordinates conjugate movement.
These connections support conjugate movements and vestibulo-ocular responses; the horizontal exam most often highlights VI-to-III communication.

title: Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO)

items.text: INO is named for the side of the impaired adducting eye; intact convergence helps show that medial rectus can still function through near pathways.
The contralateral eye abducts with nystagmus while the ipsilateral eye has impaired adduction.
The impaired adducting eye identifies the side of INO. Multiple sclerosis is a classic association in younger patients, and convergence can be preserved.
Stroke is a classic INO cause in older adults; multiple sclerosis is a common association in younger patients, especially with bilateral involvement.
An internuclear connection can be impaired while the final motor apparatus remains functional; convergence preservation is common but not universal in INO.
Ipsilateral gaze palsy plus ipsilateral INO leaves only contralateral abduction as the remaining horizontal movement.

qualifications: Convergence is often preserved in INO but is not guaranteed. Name the lesion for the side of the impaired adducting eye.

items.text: Light uses optic afference, corneal touch uses ophthalmic trigeminal afference, and rotation uses vestibular afference.
MLF coordinates ocular motor nuclei; it can produce INO without directly damaging retinal visual, V1 sensory, or pupil light-reflex pathways.
